Slides (black), the lecture notes (green — study guide written from the lecture by Mohammed Alessa, Mohammed Alsalamah & Abdulrahman Alomar) and every gift (red). Aldughaither has no urology chapter. Older exams also asked about retention, urethral stricture, urge incontinence and catheter UTI — they are at the end with added background.

King Saud University logo (title slide) (1)

1. LUTS — two families of symptoms

STORAGE (irritative)VOIDING (obstructive)
DysuriaHesitancy
FrequencyWeak stream
UrgencyStraining
IncontinenceIntermittency
NocturiaDribbling
  • LUTS is a symptom complex, not a diagnosis. Storage = filling phase — the bladder cannot hold urine comfortably (overactive, irritated, inflamed). Voiding = emptying phase — the bladder cannot empty easily (outlet obstruction or a weak detrusor).
  • Trap: symptom type does not name the cause — an obstructing prostate commonly produces storage symptoms too (detrusor hypertrophy), and a weak bladder can mimic obstruction.
  • All present with voiding LUTS except → cystitis (storage/irritative). 428 ×3 427
  • LUTS — true statement → can happen in a young female. 426

What causes LUTS?

  • Bladder: OAB (detrusor overactivity) · detrusor underactivity · neurogenic bladder dysfunction · bladder tumour · foreign body. Outlet: benign prostatic obstruction · urethral stricture. Infection/irritation: UTI · prostatitis · distal ureteric stone. Urine production: nocturnal polyuria · and others.

2. BPH — the prostate gland

  • Male sex organ · glandulo-muscular: 70% glandular, 30% fibromuscular stroma · size up to 20 cc · produces PSA · fluid component of semen.
Same anatomy image (repeated slide) (1)
  • Zones.
ZoneWhereClinical significance
Transition zone → BPHInner — wraps around the proximal urethraBPH arises here → compresses the urethra early → LUTS
Peripheral zone → cancerOuter, posterior — the largest zoneMost prostate cancers arise here; the zone you feel on DRE
Central zoneSurrounds the ejaculatory ductsLess clinically important
Anterior zoneAnterior fibromuscular stromaNon-glandular
  • Rule of thumb: inside → BPH (transition zone, hugs the urethra, symptoms early). Outside → cancer (peripheral zone, palpable on DRE, symptoms late).

Blood supply, drainage, nerves

  • Arterial: main supply from the prostatic artery ← inferior vesical ← internal iliac.
  • Venous: prostatic venous plexus → internal iliac veins; also to the internal vertebral venous plexus.

Venous drainage — prostatic and vesical plexuses to the internal iliac veins

  • Why the vertebral plexus is high-yield: this valveless connection is how prostate cancer spreads to the spine — back pain in an older man with a raised PSA suggests bone metastases.
  • Innervation: sympathetic, parasympathetic and sensory from the inferior hypogastric plexus.
  • Function: secretes a fluid which contributes to the volume of the semen.
  • Key element for prostate growth: DHT · testicular androgen · adrenal androgens.
  • Testosterone → (5α-reductase) → DHT, the key growth driver. Block the enzyme and the gland shrinks → basis of 5α-reductase inhibitors.

BPH

  • What: increased number (hyperplasia) of epithelial & stromal cells. How: epithelial and stromal proliferation or impaired programmed cell death.
  • Let's be clear: does prostate size correlate with symptoms? Do you treat every patient with an enlarged prostate?
  • No and no. A small gland can obstruct badly; a large one may cause few symptoms — treat the patient, not the ultrasound volume. Treatment is driven by bothersome symptoms and complications, not size alone.
  • BPH — the false statement → cystoscopy is done for obstructive symptoms caused by BPH (not routine). True: DRE size doesn't predict obstructive symptoms. 427 ×2
  • BPH — the false statement → immediate TURP (treatment is stepwise; surgery has indications). 426

3. Presentation & complications

  • LUTS: storage (dysuria, frequency, urgency, incontinence) · voiding (hesitancy, weak stream, straining, intermittency, dribbling).
  • Complications: bladder stones · UTI · bladder decompensation · incontinence · upper tract deterioration · haematuria · AUR.
  • Why patients develop storage LUTS: bladder hypertrophy.
  • Obstruction → detrusor works harder → bladder hypertrophy (thick, trabeculated; overactive → storage LUTS) → decompensation (poor emptying, retention).
  • Link it: the complications are almost exactly the indications for surgery — learn them once, use them twice.
  • 65-year-old, moderate storage and voiding LUTS, firm ~50 g prostate, urinalysis clean → benign prostatic hyperplasia. 439 ×2

4. Evaluation

  • History and physical examination: medical history · physical exam — abdomen · external genitalia · DRE · focused neurological exam.
  • Abdomen: palpable bladder (retention). Genitalia: meatal stenosis, phimosis. DRE: smooth and enlarged (BPH) vs hard and nodular (suspect cancer). Neuro exam excludes a neurogenic cause.
  • Investigations: urine analysis · cytology · serum Cr · PSA · US · post-void residual · uroflowmetry.
TestWhy
Urine analysisInfection, haematuria
CytologyScreens for bladder cancer with haematuria or unexplained storage symptoms
Serum creatinineHas obstruction damaged the upper tracts?
PSAProstate cancer risk; also reflects gland volume
UltrasoundProstate volume (lecture example 58 mL), bladder wall, hydronephrosis
Post-void residualBladder scan of urine left after voiding → incomplete emptying / chronic retention
UroflowmetryPeak flow (Qmax) and the shape of the curve

Post-void residual — bladder ultrasound and a portable bladder scanner

Uroflowmetry — normal bell-shaped curve (A) vs abnormal patterns; patient voiding into a flowmeter

  • Qmax > 15 mL/s is normal; < 10 mL/s suggests obstruction. Normal = bell-shaped; prostatic obstruction = low, prolonged, slow tail; urethral stricture = flat plateau ("box"); interrupted = straining / weak detrusor. A low flow can't distinguish obstruction from a weak detrusor — that needs pressure-flow urodynamics. Combine with PVR.
  • 65-year-old with reduced urine flow — the mandatory investigation → urine analysis. 438
  • Patient with both diabetes and BPH and LUTS — to tell which causes it → urodynamics (voiding diary, flow studies). 426
  • 60-year-old, mild symptoms, small prostate with nodules on DRE, normal PSA → transrectal US with biopsy. 436 ×4

5. Treatment

  • Watchful waiting · medical therapy · surgical management.
  • Ladder: watchful waiting (mild, no complications) → medical therapy (bothersome symptoms: α1-blockers, 5ARI or both) → surgery (complications or failure of medical therapy).

Watchful waiting

  • Suitable for mild symptoms · delay in treatment will not have irreversible consequences · does not mean literally WW.
  • It means education, reassurance, lifestyle advice (less evening fluid, caffeine and alcohol) and periodic review.

Medical therapy

  • α1-blockers: relaxation. 5α-reductase blockers: decrease size.
  • α-blockers: nonselective — phenoxybenzamine. α1-blockers: short acting — prazosin, indoramin, IR alfuzosin · long-acting — terazosin, doxazosin, alfuzosin SR · subtype selective — tamsulosin.
  • α1A (prostate and bladder-neck smooth muscle) — blocking it relieves dynamic obstruction: the target of tamsulosin. α1B dominates in blood vessels → blocking it causes orthostatic hypotension and dizziness.
  • Side effects: orthostatic hypotension · dizziness · syncope · tiredness (asthenia) · peripheral oedema · headache · ejaculatory problems · nasal congestion (flu-like).
  • 5α-reductase blockers: finasteride — inhibits type 2, 70% reduction in DHT. Dutasteride — inhibits types 1 & 2, 95% reduction in DHT.
Enzyme-blocking icon (decorative) (1)
  • Important to know: decrease in total gland volume 20–30% · volume regression maximal at 6 months · symptoms 2 months · PSA value should be doubled in patients on chronic (> 6 months) 5ARI.
  • Side effects: ED · decreased libido · gynaecomastia.
  • Combination therapy: α1-blockers + 5α-reductase blockers.
Two fists (combination — decorative) (1)
α1-blockers5α-reductase inhibitors
ActionRelax prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle — dynamic componentShrink the prostate by blocking DHT — static component
OnsetFast — daysSlow — symptoms ~2 months; volume max at 6 months
Gland volumeNo change↓ 20–30%
PSANo effectRoughly halved → double it after > 6 months
  • Combination = complementary actions on the dynamic + static components — typically for larger glands with bothersome symptoms.
  • 55-year-old, LUTS, normal urinalysis and PSA, low flow, 30 cc prostate, raised PVR → α-blocker. 439 ×3
  • 65-year-old, symptomatic and bothered, 60 g prostate → initial management α-blocker + 5α-reductase inhibitor. 429
  • All can be used for LUTS except → vasopressin. 426

Surgical management

  • Indications: recurrent urinary retention · recurrent UTIs · renal insufficiency · bladder calculi · recurrent gross haematuria · failure of medical therapy.
  • Types:

Open (simple) prostatectomy and transurethral resection with a resectoscope

  • TURP — resectoscope through the urethra cores out the obstructing transition-zone tissue: the standard operation. Open (simple) prostatectomy — the adenoma is enucleated through an abdominal incision, for very large glands.
  • BPH, worsening voiding symptoms — absolute indication for surgery → bladder stone formation from outlet obstruction. 438 ×4
  • BPH on tamsulosin, still symptomatic, prostate 20 g, PSA 0.2, clean urine → TURP (failure of medical therapy). 439

6. Other questions asked (not on this year's slides)

Acute and chronic retention

Added explanationAcute urinary retention — painful inability to void, tender dull suprapubic mass → urethral catheter first (suprapubic if urethral catheterization fails or is contraindicated). After draining a chronically obstructed bladder (especially with raised creatinine), watch for post-obstructive diuresis — high urine output with dehydration and electrolyte loss.
  • 72-year-old, unable to pass urine for 8 h, tender dull suprapubic mass → Foley catheter insertion. 437 ×8
  • Chronic retention with raised creatinine, catheter drained 800 mL → monitor for post-obstructive diuresis. 434 ×2

Urethral stricture

Added explanationUrethral stricture — weak stream in a man with a past history of urethral trauma, instrumentation/catheter or urethritis; flat "box" flow curve. Investigation of choice = retrograde (ascending) urethrogram (± voiding cystourethrogram) to show the site and length; treatment: dilatation or optical urethrotomy for short strictures, urethroplasty for long or recurrent ones.
  • 60-year-old with weak flow — urethrogram shows a narrowed segment → urethral stricture. 435 ×7
  • Urethral stricture — true statement → ascending urethrogram is the investigation of choice. 426

Bladder control & incontinence

Added explanationThe micturition reflex is a sacral (S2–S4) spinal reflex coordinated by the pontine micturition centre in the brainstem, under voluntary control from the cortex. Urge incontinence = leakage with a sudden urge, caused by detrusor overactivity (instability) — treated with bladder training and antimuscarinics/β3-agonists.
  • Organization of the micturition reflex → brainstem (pontine micturition centre). 436
  • Urge incontinence — cause → detrusor instability (overactivity). 426

Infections

Added explanationColovesical fistula — mostly from diverticular disease (then colon cancer, Crohn's): recurrent UTIs, pneumaturia (bubbles) and fecaluria (cloudy, debris), in a patient with left iliac fossa pain. Catheter-associated UTI — organisms enter along the catheter; risk rises with poor insertion technique/catheter care and duration.
  • 65-year-old with dysuria, cloudy urine with bubbles, recurrent left iliac fossa pain → diverticular disease (colovesical fistula). 439 ×5
  • Most common cause of catheter-associated UTI → improper catheterization technique. 436
Added explanationIn a baby with a first febrile UTI / pyelonephritis (often from VUR), the first step after treating the infection is prophylactic antibiotics while the work-up (US, VCUG) is done — surgery is for breakthrough infections or high-grade reflux. See the Antenatal hydronephrosis lecture.
  • 8-month-old with a first pyelonephritis → prophylactic antibiotics. 439
